newsitem.title: USA: Congress gears up to fight new clean air standards.
newsitem.headline: Congress gears up to fight new clean air standards.

text.p: Lawmakers are preparing for an uphill battle to kill the Clinton administration's tough new limits on smog and soot, in a fight pitting industrial states against those with tight pollution controls.
The standards, backed by President Bill Clinton this week, will tighten limits on ozone for the first time in 20 years and set curbs on fine particles for the first time.
Congressmen on both sides of the aisle quickly declared war on the administration. But they face difficult odds to stop the new rules because both parties are split on the issue.

Close to 80 House Democrats and many Republicans urged Clinton to reject the Environmental Protection Agency's air quality proposal. But other Democrats and some Republicans, including Sen. Alfonse D'Amato of New York, pressed the administration to back EPA.
Green groups assume the White House would veto any bill to stop the EPA plan, which means opponents would have to muster two-thirds majorities to override a veto.
Advocates of the new clean air standards said the odds were in their favor, because lawmakers would balk at voting against protecting public health.

"I'm not saying we've won and it's over," said Daniel Rosenberg, a staff attorney for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, which has pressed for the new limits. "But I can't imagine that they're overly confident about getting two-thirds in the House and the Senate."

"We're not terribly concerned," said David Hawkins, senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council. "We think that on an up or down vote (to overturn the standards) ... that many members of Congress will be reluctant to vote for something which the administration will say is going to decrease protection to public health."
All eyes are focused on the House, where the air standard opponents are weighing several options to overturn the rules.

They could block the agency from publishing the rules by a July 19 court-ordered deadline under a bill already offered by two Democrats and a Republican, stop the rules under a new regulatory review law, withhold funds for the EPA to carry out the rules, or attempt to change the rules.
The fight is expected to take a long time. "It's practically impossible for the Congress to pass anything quickly," a Democratic aide said.

If they fail to prevent the official publication of the rule, lawmakers could take a stab at overturning the rules as soon as they are issued, when they will have 60 working days -- essentially the rest of this Congressional year -- to review the plan.

But leaders of the fight are unsure whether to use the review process as their weapon, because the law that allows Congress to overturn regulations with a simple majority has never been tested before.
"I think it's neither necessary nor wise to take that course," said Rep. John Dingell of Michigan, a powerful Democrat who is spearheading the bid to block the standards.
Dingell said he had not counted votes yet but had talked to House and Senate Democrat and Republican leaders. "My responses as of this moment are splendid," he said in a telephone interview.
He said there was no reason to rush into legislation, because EPA would take a long time to craft ways to carry out its new rules. "This whole matter is in a very early stage."
Dingell, the biggest specter for environmental groups in this fight, predicted his side would prevail. "I think I'll do very, very well indeed," he said.
